questions.stem: Which of the following is an importance of farm animals to man?
options: Provision of animal protein such as meat, milk and eggs
questions.explanation: Livestock supply protein foods, hides and skins, manure, draught power, income and employment.

questions.stem: Farm animals classified according to their main product would place the Friesian cow in the group of
questions.explanation: The Friesian (Holstein-Friesian) is a high-yielding dairy breed.

questions.stem: Which of the following animals is a pseudo-ruminant, having a large caecum where fibre is fermented but no rumen?
questions.explanation: Rabbits and horses are hindgut fermenters (pseudo-ruminants); rabbits also practise caecotrophy.

questions.topic: Internal organs and their functions in farm animals
questions.stem: In the ruminant stomach, the compartment with a honeycomb-like lining that helps form the bolus for regurgitation is the
questions.explanation: The reticulum has a honeycomb lining and works with the rumen in cud formation; the omasum has leaf-like folds.

questions.topic: Internal organs and their functions in farm animals
questions.stem: The organ in poultry where the shell is added to the egg is the
questions.explanation: The shell is deposited in the uterus over about 20 hours; albumen is added in the magnum and shell membranes in the isthmus.

questions.topic: Body systems and their functions in farm animals
questions.stem: The system in a farm animal responsible for removing nitrogenous wastes from the blood is the
questions.explanation: Kidneys filter blood and form urine, removing urea and excess salts.

questions.topic: Reproduction in farm animals: definition of terms
questions.stem: The term "flushing" in animal reproduction refers to
options: washing the reproductive tract after birth
removing the young from the mother
feeding females on a high plane of nutrition before mating to increase ovulation rate
giving water to animals after mating
questions.explanation: Flushing improves body condition and can increase the number of ova released, e.g. in ewes and sows.

questions.topic: Reproduction in farm animals: definition of terms
questions.stem: A young female pig that has not yet given birth is called a
questions.explanation: A gilt is a young female pig before her first litter; a barrow is a castrated male.

questions.stem: The oestrous cycle of a cow lasts about
questions.explanation: Cows come on heat about every 21 days (range 18-24); 114 days is the gestation of a sow.

questions.stem: The incubation period of the eggs of the domestic fowl is
questions.explanation: Chicken eggs hatch in 21 days; duck and turkey eggs take about 28 days.

questions.stem: Candling of eggs during incubation is done to
options: increase the temperature of the eggs
detect infertile eggs and dead embryos
questions.explanation: A bright light shows developing blood vessels in fertile eggs; clear eggs are removed.

questions.stem: The hormone that causes milk let-down during suckling or milking is
questions.explanation: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary contracts the cells around the alveoli of the udder.

questions.stem: The hormone that maintains pregnancy in farm animals is
questions.explanation: Progesterone from the corpus luteum (and placenta) maintains the uterine lining and pregnancy.

questions.stem: Steaming up in dairy cattle refers to
options: feeding extra concentrate in the last weeks of pregnancy
washing the cow with hot water before calving
drying off the cow by stopping milking
giving the cow steam baths to prevent disease
questions.explanation: Extra feed before calving builds body reserves and prepares the cow for high milk yield.

questions.stem: A major disadvantage of the extensive system of keeping livestock is that
options: it requires very high capital investment
it needs a large amount of concentrate feed
animals are exposed to theft, predators, diseases and parasites
questions.explanation: Free-ranging animals are poorly protected and difficult to manage, though costs are low.

questions.stem: Docking in sheep is the
options: removal of part of the tail
questions.explanation: Docking reduces soiling of the tail area and fly strike.

questions.stem: Ear notching in pigs is mainly carried out for
questions.explanation: Notches in different positions of the ears give each pig a number.

questions.topic: Meaning and classes of animal feeds
questions.stem: Which of the following feedstuffs is an energy concentrate?
questions.explanation: Cereal grains such as maize supply mainly carbohydrates; fish meal is a protein concentrate and bone meal a mineral supplement.

questions.topic: Animal feeds and feeding: livestock rations
questions.stem: A production ration is given to animals in addition to the maintenance ration in order to
options: support growth, milk, egg or wool production
keep the animal alive without gaining weight
reduce the feed intake of the animal
prepare the animal for slaughter only
questions.explanation: Production rations supply nutrients above maintenance for growth, lactation, pregnancy or work.

questions.topic: Animal feeds and feeding: livestock rations
questions.stem: Broilers consumed 4.5 kg of feed and gained 2.5 kg live weight. The feed conversion ratio is
questions.explanation: FCR = feed consumed / weight gain = 4.5 / 2.5 = 1.8.

questions.stem: Using the Pearson square, a farmer mixes maize (10% crude protein) and soybean meal (45% crude protein) to obtain a 24% crude protein ration. The percentage of soybean meal in the ration is
questions.explanation: Maize parts = 45 - 24 = 21; soybean parts = 24 - 10 = 14; total 35. Soybean = 14/35 x 100 = 40%.

questions.topic: Processing techniques for different farm animal products
questions.stem: Pasteurisation of milk involves
options: heating milk to a moderate temperature for a set time and then cooling it quickly to destroy harmful microorganisms
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation (e.g. 72 degrees C for 15 seconds) kills pathogens with little effect on flavour.

questions.stem: A problem in the marketing of fresh milk by pastoralists in Nigeria is that
options: there is no demand for milk
milk can be stored for months without processing
milk prices are fixed by law
milk is highly perishable and cold-chain facilities are inadequate
questions.explanation: Perishability, poor roads and lack of cooling centres limit milk marketing.

questions.stem: Rotational grazing helps to
options: allow grazed paddocks to recover and reduce parasite build-up
keep animals permanently in one paddock
questions.explanation: Moving animals between paddocks rests pasture and breaks parasite cycles.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a method of rangeland improvement?
options: Introduction of improved grasses and legumes
questions.explanation: Reseeding, controlled burning, water provision, fertilising and controlled stocking improve rangeland.

questions.topic: Meaning and aims of animal improvement
questions.stem: One aim of animal improvement is to
options: produce animals with higher productivity and disease resistance
reduce the growth rate of animals
questions.explanation: Improvement seeks higher yields, better quality, faster growth and adaptability.

questions.stem: Repeatedly mating local females and their offspring to purebred exotic males over several generations is called
questions.explanation: Grading up gradually raises the proportion of exotic genes in the herd.

questions.stem: Crossbreeding is mating of animals from
options: the same breed and the same family
questions.explanation: Crossbreeding combines traits of different breeds and may give hybrid vigour.

questions.stem: Semen for artificial insemination is stored for long periods in
options: liquid nitrogen at about -196 degrees C
questions.explanation: Frozen semen in straws keeps for years in liquid nitrogen.

questions.stem: A disease that can be transmitted from animals to humans is called a
questions.explanation: Examples include anthrax, rabies, brucellosis and tuberculosis.

questions.topic: General symptoms of diseases in farm animals
questions.stem: Which of the following is a general sign of ill-health in farm animals?
options: Loss of appetite and dull, rough coat
questions.explanation: Sick animals show reduced appetite, dullness, rough coat, abnormal temperature and discharges.

questions.topic: Diseases of farm animals, prevention and control
questions.stem: Anthrax in cattle is caused by a
questions.explanation: Anthrax is bacterial; carcasses must not be opened but burned or buried deeply with lime.

questions.topic: Diseases of farm animals, prevention and control
questions.stem: Gumboro disease (infectious bursal disease) of poultry mainly damages the
options: bursa of Fabricius, weakening the immune system
questions.explanation: The virus destroys the bursa, causing immunosuppression in young chickens.

questions.topic: Factors predisposing farm animals to diseases
questions.stem: Which of the following factors predisposes farm animals to disease?
options: Overcrowding and poor ventilation in pens
questions.explanation: Stress, overcrowding, poor hygiene and poor nutrition lower resistance to disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an endoparasite of farm animals?
questions.explanation: Tapeworms live inside the gut; ticks, lice and mites live on the skin (ectoparasites).

questions.stem: Pigs become infected with the pork tapeworm (Taenia solium) mainly by
options: eating food contaminated with human faeces containing the eggs
questions.explanation: Pigs are intermediate hosts; poor sanitation allows them to eat eggs passed by infected humans.

questions.stem: Tsetse flies are important livestock pests because they
options: lay eggs in the skin of cattle
questions.explanation: Tsetse flies (Glossina) transmit trypanosomes while sucking blood.

questions.topic: Practical: products and by-products of farm animals
questions.stem: Gelatine is obtained from which by-product of farm animals?
questions.explanation: Collagen from bones and skins is boiled to extract gelatine.

questions.topic: Practical: tools and equipment used in management of farm animals
questions.stem: An elastrator is used to
options: apply rubber rings for castration or docking of young animals
questions.explanation: The elastrator stretches a rubber ring placed on the scrotum or tail, cutting off blood supply.

questions.stem: A specimen collected from a cow has a flat, leaf-shaped body and was found in the bile ducts. It is most likely
questions.explanation: Fasciola is leaf-shaped and lives in the bile ducts of the liver.

questions.topic: Internal organs and their functions in farm animals
questions.stem:
(a) Name the parts of the alimentary canal of a domestic fowl in the order in which food passes through them. [6 marks]
(b) State the function of each of the following in the fowl: (i) crop; (ii) gizzard; (iii) caeca. [6 marks]
(c) State four differences between the digestive system of a ruminant and that of a fowl. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a) Mouth/beak, oesophagus, crop, proventriculus, gizzard, small intestine (duodenum and ileum), caeca, large intestine (rectum), cloaca, vent (correct order; deduct for omissions or wrong order)
2 marks: (b)(i) Crop: temporary storage and softening/moistening of food
2 marks: (b)(ii) Gizzard: grinding of food with the help of grit, since birds have no teeth
2 marks: (b)(iii) Caeca: fermentation/digestion of some fibre by microorganisms and absorption of water
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: ruminant has teeth, fowl has beak and no teeth; ruminant has four-chambered stomach, fowl has proventriculus and gizzard; ruminant chews the cud, fowl does not; ruminant digests much cellulose by rumen microbes, fowl digests little fibre; fowl has crop and cloaca, ruminant has none; ruminant has long intestine relative to body, fowl short; fowl has paired caeca
questions.explanation: (a) Beak and mouth, oesophagus, crop, proventriculus, gizzard, small intestine, caeca, large intestine, cloaca and vent. (b) The crop stores and softens food; the gizzard grinds it using grit; the caeca ferment some fibre and absorb water. (c) Ruminants have teeth, a four-chambered stomach, chew the cud and digest cellulose by rumen microbes; fowls have a beak, crop, proventriculus, gizzard, cloaca and digest little fibre.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the female reproductive system of a cow, stating the function of each part. [10 marks]
(b) State four signs that a cow is about to give birth. [4 marks]
(c) Describe how a newborn calf should be cared for in its first week. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Ovaries: produce ova and hormones (oestrogen, progesterone)
2 marks: (a) Oviducts (fallopian tubes)/infundibulum: receive ova; site of fertilisation
2 marks: (a) Uterus (horns and body): implantation and development of the foetus; placenta formation
2 marks: (a) Cervix: closes the uterus during pregnancy (mucus plug); opens at birth
2 marks: (a) Vagina and vulva: receive the penis/semen during mating and form the birth canal
4 marks: (b) Any four, 1 mark each: enlarged udder filled with milk (bagging up); swollen, relaxed vulva with mucus discharge; relaxation of pelvic ligaments (sunken tail head); restlessness and isolation from the herd; frequent lying down and getting up; loss of appetite
6 marks: (c) Any six, 1 mark each: clear mucus from nose and mouth to help breathing; dip navel in iodine; ensure calf suckles colostrum within the first few hours; keep in clean, dry, warm pen; identify (tag/record); observe for diarrhoea and illness; weigh and record birth weight; protect from predators and bad weather
questions.explanation: (a) The ovaries produce ova and hormones; the oviducts are the site of fertilisation; the uterus holds the developing foetus; the cervix seals the uterus during pregnancy; the vagina and vulva receive semen and form the birth canal. (b) Udder enlargement, swollen vulva with discharge, sunken tail head, restlessness and loss of appetite. (c) Clear the airways, disinfect the navel, ensure colostrum feeding early, keep the calf warm and dry, identify it and watch for illness.

questions.stem:
(a) Define (i) balanced ration; (ii) maintenance ration. [4 marks]
(b) A farmer wants to prepare 200 kg of a growers' ration containing 16% crude protein using maize (9% CP) and groundnut cake (44% CP). Use the Pearson square to calculate the quantity of each ingredient. [10 marks]
(c) State three factors to consider when formulating a livestock ration. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) A ration that supplies all the nutrients required by the animal in the right proportions and amounts for 24 hours
2 marks: (a)(ii) The amount of feed needed to keep the animal alive and maintain its body weight without production
2 marks: (b) Pearson square with 16 in the centre, maize 9 and groundnut cake 44 at the corners
2 marks: (b) Maize parts = 44 - 16 = 28; groundnut cake parts = 16 - 9 = 7
2 marks: (b) Total parts = 35
2 marks: (b) Maize = 28/35 x 200 = 160 kg
2 marks: (b) Groundnut cake = 7/35 x 200 = 40 kg
6 marks: (c) Any three, 2 marks each: nutrient requirement of the animal (species, age, purpose); nutrient composition of available feedstuffs; cost and availability of ingredients; palatability; presence of anti-nutritional factors/toxins; digestibility
questions.explanation: (a) A balanced ration supplies all required nutrients in correct proportions for a day; a maintenance ration only keeps the animal alive at constant weight. (b) Maize parts = 44 - 16 = 28; groundnut cake parts = 16 - 9 = 7; total 35. Maize = 28/35 x 200 = 160 kg; groundnut cake = 40 kg. Check: (160 x 9 + 40 x 44)/200 = 16%. (c) Animal requirements, nutrient content of feeds, cost and availability, palatability and absence of toxins.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between natural pasture and established (sown) pasture. [4 marks]
(b) Name two grasses and two legumes suitable for establishing pasture in West Africa. [4 marks]
(c) Describe four practices in the management of an established pasture. [8 marks]
(d) State four effects of overgrazing. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) Natural pasture: grassland that develops naturally without being planted, often of mixed quality
2 marks: (a) Established pasture: land deliberately planted with selected grasses and/or legumes and managed for grazing
2 marks: (b) Grasses, any two: Panicum maximum (guinea grass); Pennisetum purpureum (elephant grass); Andropogon gayanus (gamba grass); Cynodon (star grass); Brachiaria
2 marks: (b) Legumes, any two: Centrosema pubescens; Stylosanthes; Pueraria phaseoloides; Calopogonium mucunoides; Leucaena leucocephala
8 marks: (c) Any four, 2 marks each: rotational grazing/paddocking; controlled stocking rate; fertiliser application; weed control; irrigation in dry season; reseeding of bare patches; controlled burning; conservation of excess as hay or silage; provision of water points
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: destruction of palatable species; exposure of soil to erosion; invasion by unpalatable weeds; low animal productivity/weight loss; build-up of parasites; soil compaction; desertification
questions.explanation: (a) Natural pasture develops on its own; established pasture is sown with selected species. (b) Guinea grass and elephant grass; Centrosema and Stylosanthes. (c) Rotational grazing, correct stocking rate, fertilising, weed control, reseeding and conserving surplus as hay or silage. (d) Overgrazing destroys good species, exposes soil to erosion, allows weeds to invade, lowers animal performance and increases parasites.

questions.stem:
(a) What is artificial insemination? [2 marks]
(b) Describe the steps involved in artificial insemination of a cow. [8 marks]
(c) State four advantages and two disadvantages of artificial insemination. [6 marks]
(d) Name four items of equipment used in artificial insemination. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) The deliberate introduction of semen collected from a male into the reproductive tract of a female by artificial means rather than natural mating
2 marks: (b) Collect semen from a proven bull using an artificial vagina
2 marks: (b) Evaluate (volume, motility, concentration), dilute with extender and store (chilled or frozen in liquid nitrogen in straws)
2 marks: (b) Detect heat in the cow; thaw the semen straw in warm water and load the insemination gun
2 marks: (b) Restrain the cow; pass the gun through the vagina and cervix (recto-vaginal method) and deposit semen in the uterus at the right time (about 12 hours after onset of heat)
4 marks: (c) Advantages, any four, 1 mark each: one bull can serve many cows; spreads superior genes widely; reduces cost of keeping bulls; reduces spread of venereal diseases; semen can be stored and transported over long distances; allows use of semen after the bull dies; avoids injury from heavy bulls
2 marks: (c) Disadvantages, any two, 1 mark each: requires skilled personnel; expensive equipment; heat detection must be accurate; risk of spreading defects if bull is not tested; poor hygiene can spread disease
4 marks: (d) Any four, 1 mark each: artificial vagina; insemination gun/catheter; liquid nitrogen container (flask); semen straws; microscope; speculum; thermometer; protective gloves
questions.explanation: (a) AI is the placing of collected semen into the female tract without natural mating. (b) Semen is collected with an artificial vagina, evaluated, diluted and frozen in straws; when the cow is on heat, a thawed straw is loaded into a gun and passed through the cervix to deposit semen in the uterus. (c) AI spreads superior genes widely, saves bull costs and limits venereal disease, but needs skilled staff, equipment and accurate heat detection. (d) Artificial vagina, insemination gun, liquid nitrogen flask and straws.

questions.topic: Diseases of farm animals, prevention and control
questions.stem:
(a) For each of the following diseases, state the causal organism, mode of transmission, two symptoms and one method of control: (i) foot-and-mouth disease; (ii) peste des petits ruminants (PPR) of goats; (iii) African swine fever. [15 marks]
(b) State five ways of preventing disease outbreaks on a livestock farm. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a)(i) FMD: virus (aphthovirus)
1 mark: (a)(i) Transmission: contact with infected animals, saliva, contaminated feed, water, equipment and people; airborne
2 marks: (a)(i) Symptoms: blisters (vesicles) in mouth, on feet and teats; excessive salivation; lameness; fever; drop in milk yield (any two)
1 mark: (a)(i) Control: vaccination; quarantine and movement control; slaughter of infected animals
1 mark: (a)(ii) PPR: virus (morbillivirus)
1 mark: (a)(ii) Transmission: close contact, discharges from eyes, nose and mouth, contaminated feed and water
2 marks: (a)(ii) Symptoms: high fever; discharges from eyes and nose; mouth sores; diarrhoea; pneumonia/coughing; death (any two)
1 mark: (a)(ii) Control: vaccination; isolation of sick animals; quarantine
1 mark: (a)(iii) ASF: virus (asfivirus)
1 mark: (a)(iii) Transmission: contact with infected pigs, pork products, swill feeding, contaminated equipment, soft ticks
2 marks: (a)(iii) Symptoms: high fever; reddening/blue discoloration of skin (ears, belly); loss of appetite; bloody diarrhoea; sudden death (any two)
1 mark: (a)(iii) Control: no effective vaccine generally available; strict biosecurity, no swill feeding, slaughter and safe disposal of infected herds, quarantine
5 marks: (b) Any five, 1 mark each: vaccination; quarantine new stock; isolate sick animals; good sanitation and disinfection; footbath at farm entrance; restrict visitors; balanced feeding; avoid overcrowding; proper disposal of dead animals; regular veterinary checks
questions.explanation: (a) FMD is viral, spread by contact and contaminated materials, causing blisters, salivation and lameness; controlled by vaccination and movement control. PPR is viral, spread by contact and discharges, causing fever, discharges, mouth sores and diarrhoea; controlled by vaccination and isolation. African swine fever is viral, spread by infected pigs, pork, swill and ticks, causing fever, skin discoloration and sudden death; it is controlled mainly by strict biosecurity and culling. (b) Vaccination, quarantine, isolation, sanitation, footbaths and restricting visitors.
